item.title: C Char Size Variations Across Architectures: A Deep Dive
item.description:
“C Char Size Variations Across Architectures: A Deep Dive”

The char data type in C and C++ is fundamental, but its underlying size isn’t as universally fixed as one might assume. While modern systems predominantly use an 8-bit char, historical computing architectures and specialized processors, such as Digital Signal Processors (DSPs), have employed different bit configurations for char. This raises critical questions about code portability and the assumptions we make about data types.

item.title: x86 Assembly Registers: EAX, AX, AH, AL Explained
item.description:
“x86 Assembly Registers: EAX, AX, AH, AL Explained”

When working with x86 assembly, a common point of exploration involves the relationship between the 32-bit EAX register and its constituent parts: AX (the lower 16 bits), AH (the upper 8 bits of AX), and AL (the lower 8 bits of AX). How do these registers interact, and what are the implications of accessing them individually?

The structure of these registers is hierarchical. EAX represents the full 32-bit value. AX is a subset, containing the lower 16 bits of EAX. AL is the least significant byte (bits 0-7) of AX (and thus of EAX), while AH comprises bits 8-15 of AX (the upper half of AX, or the second byte of EAX).

item.title: Caller-Saved vs Callee-Saved Registers: Understanding Function Call Conventions
item.description:
“Caller-Saved vs Callee-Saved Registers: Understanding Function Call Conventions”

When delving into the intricacies of assembly language and low-level programming, a fundamental concept revolves around how functions manage their data and interact with each other. This is primarily governed by calling conventions, which dictate how arguments are passed, return values are handled, and importantly, how processor registers are utilized and preserved across function calls. Two key categories of registers emerge from this: caller-saved and callee-saved registers.
